lesson.title: Why You Have to Subtract the Overlap
lesson.summary: The general addition rule, P(A or B) equals P(A) plus P(B) minus P(A and B), corrects for double counting the overlap region that a Venn diagram shows sitting inside both circles at once.
lesson.body:
You already know the addition rule for mutually exclusive events: if A and B cannot happen at the same time, so their circles on a Venn diagram never overlap, then P(A or B) is simply P(A) plus P(B). But most pairs of events do overlap, and adding their probabilities directly double counts whatever is shared. The general addition rule fixes this: P(A or B) equals P(A) plus P(B) minus P(A and B).

Look again at a Venn diagram with two overlapping circles. P(A) covers the entire A circle, including the lens shaped overlap. P(B) covers the entire B circle, also including that same overlap. Adding P(A) and P(B) therefore counts every point in the overlap twice, once as part of A and again as part of B. Subtracting P(A and B), the probability of that overlap, removes the duplicate and leaves each region counted exactly once.

Continue the Spanish and French example. P(Spanish) is 20 out of 50, which is 0.40. P(French) is 15 out of 50, which is 0.30. P(Spanish and French) is 8 out of 50, which is 0.16. The general addition rule gives P(Spanish or French) equals 0.40 plus 0.30 minus 0.16, which is 0.54. You can verify this directly from the diagram: the union region held 12 plus 7 plus 8 equals 27 students out of 50, and 27 divided by 50 is also 0.54. The formula and the picture agree exactly, which is the whole point of building the Venn diagram first.

Notice what happens when A and B are mutually exclusive: P(A and B) is 0, since the circles never overlap, and the general addition rule collapses to P(A or B) equals P(A) plus P(B), the simple addition rule you already knew. The simple rule is not a separate fact to memorize, it is just the special case of the general rule when there is nothing to subtract.
